oneliner.t: Democratic Iowa state representative from Council Bluffs since 2023 and two-time Paralympic gold medalist in wheelchair basketball, who won the June 2, 2026 Democratic primary for Iowa's open U.S. Senate seat.

upbringing.t: Born in Council Bluffs with spina bifida. He has used a wheelchair since childhood, and his campaign says he had 21 surgeries by age 12. His father, John, served in the Navy during the Vietnam War and later was a vocational-school administrator; Turek links his condition to his father's Agent Orange exposure. His mother, Luellen, was a social worker and community-college instructor. He grew up with three sisters and a brother; an older sister died as a toddler before he was born. He started wheelchair basketball in seventh grade, graduated from Abraham Lincoln High School, and played college wheelchair basketball at Southwest Minnesota State.

education.school: Abraham Lincoln High School, Council Bluffs

career.role: Professional wheelchair basketball player (Italy, France, Spain); U.S. national team, four Paralympics (2004–2021), gold in 2016 and 2020 (Tokyo, held 2021), bronze in 2012
career.org: European clubs incl. Bidaideak Bilbao; USA Wheelchair Basketball

career.role: Fitted patients for wheelchairs and handled insurance coverage

platform.t: Supports a public option and restoring ACA subsidies; would reverse the 2025 law's Medicaid cuts and repeal the One Big Beautiful Bill Act but keep its tax cuts on tips and overtime.
End Trump's tariffs (says he would vote on day one to end them); sponsor federal right-to-repair for farm equipment; year-round E15; mandatory country-of-origin labeling.
Opposes raising the retirement age; would apply the payroll tax to all income above the $184,500 cap.
Supports federal law restoring Roe v. Wade's protections; criticizes Iowa's six-week ban.
Close loopholes for billionaires and big corporations; raise taxes on the top 1% to fund the safety net.
Pass the PRO Act; end subminimum wages for people with disabilities; higher minimum wage.
Term limits for Congress and the Supreme Court; campaign against corruption and dark money.
Strengthen the border and simplify an earned pathway to citizenship.
Said in Aug. 2025 that U.S. aid to Israel should be limited over civilian harm in Gaza; calls the 2026 Iran war 'unnecessary'; keep the National Guard out of combat unless Congress declares war.
Reverse cuts to VA staffing and health care; supports adaptive sports for disabled veterans.

promises.t: Vote to end Trump's tariff policy on his first day in the Senate.
Visit all 99 Iowa counties every year (the 'full Grassley').
Repeal the One Big Beautiful Bill Act's health cuts while keeping no tax on tips and overtime.
Oppose any increase in the Social Security retirement age.

claims.claim: Won his first Iowa House race by six votes in a seat Trump carried twice.
claims.short: Won first race by six votes

said.where: campaign website as quoted by Ballotpedia News

record.t: A 2022 recount requested by Republican Sarah Abdouch confirmed his six-vote win (about 6,800 votes cast). The district has voted Republican for president in every election since 1968.

claims.claim: Re-elected by five points while Trump won the seat by eight.

said.where: campaign website as quoted by Ballotpedia News

record.t: Won 52.5%–47.5% in 2024. Trump's margin in the district was not independently checked.
Won team gold in Rio 2016 and Tokyo 2020 and bronze in London 2012.

said.where: campaign website as cited by Carroll Times Herald

record.t: Wikipedia confirms multiple childhood surgeries for spina bifida, but no independent record gives the count.

claims.claim: His spina bifida is linked to his father's Agent Orange exposure in Vietnam.

said.where: campaign website as cited by Carroll Times Herald

record.t: His father's Navy service in the Vietnam War is documented. The medical link is his own account.

claims.claim: First permanently disabled member of the Iowa Legislature.

record.t: Wikipedia describes him as the legislature's first permanently disabled member.

claims.claim: Named one of the most effective bipartisan state lawmakers (Center for Effective Lawmaking).

record.t: The Center for Effective Lawmaking report itself was not checked.

claims.claim: Hinson's family wealth has grown 15-fold since she entered Congress.

record.t: Disclosure values are ranges, so estimates vary: Heartland Signal (a progressive outlet) said up to tenfold, the DSCC said up to $7M, and the campaign itself said tenfold in June. NOTUS documents a $1M+ 2021 sale and a $1M–$5M spousal holding. The disclosures were not opened in this pass.

claims.claim: Hinson voted seven times to continue the Iran war.

said.where: Iowa PBS debate; repeated in releases (Sept. 2026)

record.t: She did vote against Iran war-powers resolutions, including in September 2026. Those were votes against measures to end U.S. involvement, not votes to authorize the war. A Community Note cited by Newsweek counted four such votes as of Sept. 22; the count of seven was not verified.

claims.claim: Hinson voted five times for tariffs that hurt farmers.

record.t: The specific roll calls were not identified or checked.

claims.claim: Hinson took $50,000 in taxpayer money while being a multimillionaire.

record.t: Hinson said the amount is a lawmaker per diem payable only on session days. Not checked against House records.

said.t: Said he wants 'all dark money groups' out of politics, and that VoteVets is a super PAC that chose to back him and that his campaign cannot coordinate with it.

did.t: Promoted and attended a May 1 'Veterans Happy Hour' run by VoteVets Action Fund (the group's nonprofit arm) while the Iowa House voted. VoteVets spent about $10.8M supporting him and gave his campaign $10,000. The campaign said the event was not a fundraiser.

said.t: Campaign site pledges to address Iowa's water-quality crisis, including funding water-quality sensors.

did.t: Missed the House vote (65–21) on an appropriations bill projected to fund about $320M in water-quality work over 12 years, including about $3.5M for monitoring, and missed final passage the next day.

entries.t: In the Iowa House, backed a failed amendment conditioning support for Israel on adherence to international humanitarian law, then voted for the final pro-Israel resolution without it. His campaign declined to comment on suspending arms sales.
Said U.S. aid to Israel should be limited, citing civilian harm in Gaza.
Supports continuing enhanced ACA subsidies; wants a public option.
Said he has no interest in impeaching Trump; praised parts of the 2025 tax law (no tax on tips, overtime, Social Security).

checks.legal: Courts: CourtListener, Justia and Iowa Courts Online were not searched (this tool can only open pages surfaced by web search, and the search budget was used up). No lawsuits, charges or ethics actions appeared in the reporting reviewed (AP, Iowa Capital Dispatch, Free Beacon, Newsweek, Wikipedia). The Iowa House Ethics Committee was not checked.
checks.foreign: FARA bulk files exact-name check (no match). Senate eFD not reached. His spouse is an immigrant from the Dominican Republic (biographical, not a financial tie); no foreign-government or foreign-business ties were found in reporting.
checks.claims: The campaign site's /about and /platform pages could not be opened (fetch tool blocked any URL not surfaced by search). The sample used is: campaign-site bio claims as quoted by Ballotpedia News and the Carroll Times Herald, platform items as recorded by OnTheIssues (March 2026, matching the Feb. 27, 2026 platform rollout), and his recurring debate and ad claims (Hinson wealth, Iran votes, tariffs, per diem). 11 claims, 9 of them checkable facts.
checks.democracy: No certification votes (not in Congress in 2017 or 2021). His public statements on the 2020 and 2024 results were not specifically searched.

recordx.note: PolitiFact (via Newsweek): missed 261 of 445 votes in 2026 and 9.8% in 2025, about 81% attendance since 2023. These are state-legislature figures, not Congress. Disclosure timeliness (Senate eFD) and FEC notices (RFAI) were not checked because both sites were blocked.

corp.t: No corporation-connected PACs appear in his FEC committee records. Trade/professional money: the American Association for Justice PAC (trial lawyers' association; FEC org type 'membership') gave $10,000. Labor-union PACs gave about $62,500 (IBEW, AFSCME, AFT, NEA, Machinists, Carpenters and others). Not counted here: leadership PACs of Democratic senators (about $266,500) and VoteVets' $10.8M in outside support.

lobby.t: J Street PAC gave $1,500 directly (Jan. 2026); J Street endorsed him. No AIPAC PAC or United Democracy Project money found.

research_notes: MONEY: Totals are from the provided FEC record for S6IA00298, his only federal candidacy, through 2026-06-30. Ballotpedia News says he 'raised $3.91 million as of June 30', but that figure is FEC disbursements; receipts were $6.28M. The PAC detail (leadership $266,500; labor $62,500; party $95,837 including $33,837 in DSCC coordinated spending; membership $14,325; hybrid/super PAC $43,500; ideological $33,755) covers committee filings through early Oct. 2026, so it does not add up to the 6/30 'pac_all' figure. Committee contributions began in Jan. 2026 (e.g., J Street PAC, Smart Solutions PAC). An Iowa Capital Dispatch June 2026 note that his campaign 'has not directly received PAC money' does not match the FEC records. OUTSIDE: Figures are from the provided FEC IE record (filings through Oct. 11, 2026). VoteVets' $9.76M was nearly all before the primary. SLF's $28.4M against him is mostly Sept.–Oct. media buys. The 'support' entries by AFP Action and SLF PAC that appear in the raw file are actually oppose entries mislabeled as 24A contributions and are not counted as support. MISSED VOTES: The May 1, 2026 VoteVets event is documented by the Free Beacon, a conservative outlet, from House records and the event page; his spokesman blamed rescheduling for the veterans-bill absence.
